paras: The Socorro Committee of Safety hostage-taking was the armed seizure, on December 28, 1880, of the sheriff of Socorro, New Mexico Territory, his deputy and members of the Baca family by a citizens' committee seeking the alleged killers of newspaper editor A. M. Conklin. One hostage, Antonio Maria Baca, was shot dead under the committee's guard, and federal troops were sent to protect property. Newspapers framed the episode as a near 'war of races' between the town's American and Mexican residents.

Conklin, editor of the Socorro Sun, was shot dead on the steps of the Methodist church as he and his wife left a Christmas festival. A Socorro correspondent traced the quarrel to Conklin, an usher, telling a young man to take his foot off a bench, and a coroner's jury heard that one of the young men showed a pistol at the door. The Santa Fe wire named Jacob Baca as the killer, said no justice of the peace could be found to arrest him, and reported that 'The assailants of Conklin are guarded by 2000 Mexicans.'

According to the Las Vegas Gazette, a committee of safety formed on the evening of the funeral, collected forty-three signatures on Monday and chose Col. E. W. Eaton as president. When Sheriff Garcia would not serve warrants on the three Baca brothers, first asking for them in Spanish and then shutting his door on the party, the committee 'resolved to strike for hostages.'

Early on Tuesday the armed party kicked in the sheriff's door and took him and his deputy, Felipe Baca, toward Cuba, a village about a mile and a half below Socorro where the brothers' father lived. On the way, two of its detachments mistook each other for the enemy and exchanged fifteen or twenty shots without injury. At the Baca house Eaton placed the sheriff and deputy in front of his men, set a crew to undermine the walls with picks, and falsely announced that giant powder was in place, after which twelve men and boys surrendered.

Five men were held as hostages in a guarded wine room in Socorro: the sheriff, the deputy, Antonio Maria Baca, former probate judge Dionicio Jaramillo, and Estevan Baca. A Mexican committee negotiated during the day, about thirty armed men arrived from San Marcial under Capt. Harry Hill, and four hostages were released on bonds, two of them for malfeasance and two for complicity. The committee kept Antonio Maria Baca, whom it now identified as one of the killers although the coroner's verdict had named Mesices Baca.

In the Gazette's account, when guards Dr. Dobbins and Jack Thatcher entered the room that night, Baca fired a small revolver, wounding Thatcher in the breast, and Baca was shot through the head and killed. Roundups repeated that he had procured a revolver and was killed by another guard; no other version of the shooting appears.

Company G, 18th Infantry, reached Socorro the next morning and guarded the post office and railway property, while the town was reported quiet. No report of an inquest into Antonio Maria Baca's death or of charges against his guards was found. Texas Rangers arrested Abran and Mesias Baca at Ysleta in February 1881, and a Baca was later indicted for Conklin's murder. After a Baca was acquitted of complicity in November 1881, a Socorro mob with a noose gave prosecutor Frank Chavez five minutes to leave town.

The Santa Fe wire of December 28 ran widely, in the Wheeling Intelligencer under 'The Epidemic of Crime', saying the citizens, 'finding no recourse at law', held the sheriff by force. The Wilmington Daily Gazette headed its dispatch 'A Race Conflict in New Mexico', and a Nevada paper said 'white women and children all left the town'. A Sacramento dispatch called the Mexican residents 'greasers', and Chicago's Tribune predicted that the Bacas arrested in Texas would 'probably be lynched'.

The Las Vegas Gazette sent a reporter, whose account, drawn from the committee's leaders, praised 'the Determined Men of Socorro' and blamed a telegraph operator for spreading false rumors of five lynchings. The Indiana State Sentinel, where Conklin had once worked, covered the murder at length but not the hostage-taking.

bases: An armed citizens' committee of safety seized the sheriff, his deputy and members of the Baca family as hostages and one hostage was shot dead under its guard (A4, A14, A15); no paper describes a Black victim or Black participant.

The Santa Fe wire, the Wilmington dispatch and the Las Vegas Gazette reporter's on-site account independently agree that citizens seized and held the sheriff and others after he would not arrest Conklin's alleged killers (A4, A6, A14), and the killing of the detained Baca appears in the Gazette and in later roundups (A15, A18, A19).

accounts.label: Santa Fe wire
accounts.gist: Authorities refused to arrest Conklin's murderer, so citizens 'finding no recourse at law' seized and held the sheriff and four others including the murderer; a rescue and bloodshed were feared.

accounts.label: Gazette reporter, from the committee's officers
accounts.gist: The committee demanded warrants, then seized the sheriff and deputy, besieged the Baca house at Cuba, held five hostages, released four on bonds and kept Antonio Maria Baca, who fired on entering guards and was shot dead.

accounts.label: News roundups
accounts.gist: Antoine M. Baca, a prisoner of the citizens, procured a revolver, shot a guard and was killed by another guard.

framing.detail: The wire said the citizens found 'no recourse at law', and the Las Vegas Gazette praised 'the Determined Men of Socorro' and said Socorro had been 'horribly maligned'.
Eastern and western dailies ran the Santa Fe wire under headings such as 'The Epidemic of Crime' and 'A Race Conflict in New Mexico'.
Weekly roundups reported the killing of the detained Baca in a single sentence as an act of a guard after Baca shot first.

record_check.dossier: Conklin was the murder victim whose killing prompted the episode; the victims of this episode were the five hostages, chiefly Antonio Maria Baca, who was killed.
The hostages are described as Mexican; no Black person appears in any report.
One: Antonio Maria Baca, shot dead while held by the committee.
One committee guard, Jack Thatcher, wounded.
The hostages were seized from their homes, not from officers; the sheriff himself was a hostage.
